claim: A message crossed ~2,000 km of mountains in about a week (Quito to Cusco in a week).
note: Quito–Cusco is ~2,000 km straight-line and more by road. Chroniclers claimed ~5 days Cusco–Lima and up to ~240 km/day; a week for Quito–Cusco is an estimate, not a documented fact. Also 'couldn't write a single word' is fine, but khipu may have encoded some information.
fix: A message could reportedly cross about two thousand kilometers of mountains in roughly a week or so, according to Spanish chroniclers.

claim: The Andes are the longest mountain range on Earth.
note: Continental range ~7,000 km. (Mid-ocean ridge is longer, but it is underwater.)

claim: Inca empire had ~10 million people.
note: Estimates range ~4–15 million; 10 million is common.
fix: 'Maybe ten million' (used in the later line; hedge the opening too).

claim: No paper, no ink, no wheels.
note: No writing system, no wheeled transport in practice (wheeled toys existed elsewhere in the Americas, not used for transport).

claim: Quito, Ecuador, was at the empire's northern edge; an official sent news from the frontier.
note: Quito was an important northern center, but the northern limit was further north (around Pasto/Ancasmayo, southern Colombia border). The 'bad news' scene is invented illustration. Also on-screen 'QUITO, ECUADOR' pin is ok.
fix: 'in Quito, in modern Ecuador, in the empire's far north.' Frame the official as an imagined example.

claim: The Inca had no writing.
note: Mainstream view; some scholars argue khipus (and tocapu designs) may be a form of writing/logosyllabic record.
fix: 'no writing as we usually know it.'

claim: Khipu: one main cord with dozens of strings, knots; position gives value in ones, tens, hundreds; decimal system; cotton and wool.
note: Base-10 positional; materials cotton and camelid (llama/alpaca) wool. Some khipus have hundreds or thousands of strings.

claim: Color mattered, maybe for goods, places or people; nobody has fully cracked the code.
note: Properly hedged.

claim: Chasqui were the empire's fastest messenger.
note: Fine. Note: chasqui carried khipus and oral messages.

claim: The Qhapaq Ñan is 'a paved path'.
note: Only portions were paved or stone-built; many sections were dirt tracks.
fix: 'a road, paved with stone in places'.

claim: Network stretched ~40,000 km by some counts; UNESCO lists ~30,000 km.
note: Commonly cited ~40,000 km; UNESCO's World Heritage listing covers 308 components, ~6,000 km of road, while the Qhapaq Ñan Andean Road System is described as ~30,000 km of road network identified. So 'UNESCO lists around thirty thousand' is wrong-ish: 30,000 km is the length identified by the six countries; the inscribed property is ~6,000 km.
fix: 'about forty thousand kilometers by some counts; the six countries have identified around thirty thousand, and about six thousand kilometers are UNESCO-inscribed.'

claim: 'Enough to circle the Earth.'
note: Earth's circumference is ~40,075 km, so 40,000 km only just matches, and 30,000 km does not. Contradicts the hedge just given.
fix: 'Close to the distance around the Earth, on the highest estimate.' Or cut.

claim: Roads ran from Ecuador through Peru and Bolivia into Chile and Argentina.
note: Also Colombia (southern tip). Six countries: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru.

claim: Two great roads: one through the mountains, one along the dry Pacific coast.
note: Highland road and coastal road, with many cross links.

claim: Relay huts every couple of kilometers.
note: Chasqui posts (chaskiwasi) spacing is reported at ~2.5 km (1.5 mi) up to roughly 6 km by different sources.

claim: A conch shell (pututu) shriek announced the runner.
note: Pututu conch is attested for chasquis, per chroniclers (e.g., Guaman Poma); fine, though sources vary on the exact use.
fix: 'a conch trumpet, the pututu, could signal his approach'.

claim: Message spoken aloud and the cord handed over.
note: Consistent with chroniclers.

claim: Spanish chroniclers said news could cover ~240 km a day; beats a horse over a week.
note: Figures of 240 km/day appear in some accounts and are often seen as upper-end; the horse-relay comparison is a stretch. A single horse can't match it, but relay horse systems (e.g., Mongol yam, Pony Express ~320 km/day) could.
fix: 'up to roughly 240 km a day, faster than a single horse over many days.' On-screen '240 KM A DAY' should say 'up to'.

claim: Grass suspension bridges: twisted straw ropes as thick as a leg, bridge 30 m or more.
note: Made of q'oya grass (ichu), twisted into cables; main cables up to about a human torso/thigh width — 'as thick as a leg' ok-ish. Q'eswachaka is ~30 m. Famous Apurímac bridge historically ~45 m.
fix: 'ropes as thick as a person's leg or more, bridges from 30 to 45 meters or longer'. Say 'grass' not 'straw'.

claim: Every year communities cut down and rewove a new bridge; a yearly duty.
note: True for Q'eswachaka today; assumed for Inca times via mit'a-like obligation. Sources say communities rebuilt periodically/annually.
fix: 'Communities rebuilt them regularly, about yearly, as a labor duty.'

claim: Road climbs past 4,000 m; thin air.
note: Roads reached over 5,000 m in places.

claim: Engineers cut stairs into rock and built retaining walls against landslides.
note: Documented: stairs, drainage, retaining walls.

claim: The road wasn't built for carts, but for feet and llamas.
note: Stairs make wheeled traffic impossible in places.

claim: Tambos about a day's walk apart.
note: Commonly cited ~ every 20–30 km (a day's walk) but varied with terrain.
fix: 'roughly a day's walk apart, depending on terrain'.

claim: Storehouses (qollqas) held maize, dried potatoes (chuño), sandals, spears; an army could march and never go hungry.
note: Well documented; slight overstatement.

claim: Khipukamayuq trained for years; tracked harvests, herds, soldiers, taxes.
note: Fine.

claim: The Inca had no money; tax was labor called mit'a.
note: Correct. Mit'a was rotational labor service.

claim: In return the state fed you, opened storehouses in bad years; bought loyalty.
note: Reciprocity model; historians debate extent, hedged with 'historians think'.

claim: A week after Quito the cord reaches Cusco, in the southern Andes.
note: Cusco is in the southern Peruvian Andes; ok, but timing unproven.

claim: Inca stonework: you can't slip a blade between blocks.
note: Classic hyperbole, true of the best masonry; not all Inca walls.
fix: 'in the finest walls, blocks fit so tightly that a blade barely fits'.

claim: Every road met at Cusco.
note: Four main roads (suyus) radiated from Cusco, but not every road, e.g. the coastal road bypassed it.
fix: 'the main roads radiated from Cusco's plaza'.

claim: Tawantinsuyu = 'Four Parts Together'; Cusco was its navel.
note: Cusco = 'navel' in Quechua tradition (qosqo, often translated that way, though etymology debated).

claim: Sapa Inca listens as khipukamayuq reads the cord aloud.
note: Plausible, reconstructed scene.

claim: Some khipus may record names, places, sounds; scholars argue.
note: Hedged properly. (Sabine Hyland's Collata work suggests phonetic/narrative.)

claim: Spanish writers said keepers recited whole histories from memory.
note: Reasonable summary of chronicles.

claim: Lake Titicaca at nearly 4,000 m with reed boats.
note: 3,812 m. Reed boats still used.

claim: Atacama is the driest desert on Earth; road crosses it as a thin line of stones.
note: Often called the driest non-polar desert; Antarctic Dry Valleys are drier.

claim: Road reaches Chile's Maule River, the southern edge of the empire, thousands of kilometers from Quito.
note: Maule is the traditional southern limit. Quito to Maule is ~5,000 km straight-line? About 4,500+ km; 'thousands' OK.

claim: Mapuche stopped the Inca at the Maule (battle of the Maule).
note: Traditional account; the Mapuche/Promaucae resisted. Hedged with 'historians think'.
fix: 'Here, according to chroniclers, the Mapuche and allied peoples halted the advance.' On-screen image uses Mapuche warriors; ok.

claim: In under a century the Inca grew from a small valley kingdom to ~10 million people, 'FROM 1438'.
note: Pachacuti's expansion starts ~1438 (traditional date), conquest to 1532 is 94 years. Dates are traditional and contested by archaeology.

claim: They spoke dozens of languages; the state taught Quechua and moved whole villages (mitma).
note: Mitmaq resettlement documented. Caption 'ONE LANGUAGE' is fine.

claim: 1532 Pizarro arrives with fewer than 200 soldiers and horses.
note: ~168 men, ~62 horses.

claim: Disease had already run ahead and two Inca brothers were fighting a civil war.
note: Smallpox/other epidemic likely preceded; Huáscar vs Atahualpa. Often debated whether the epidemic was smallpox.

claim: At Cajamarca the Spanish captured Atahualpa; head of system gone within days.
note: Captured on 16 Nov 1532 in one afternoon; the 'within days' is loose. Killed in 1533. Not 'gone within days'.
fix: 'In one afternoon at Cajamarca, the Spanish captured Atahualpa; he was executed in 1533.'

claim: The Spanish marched down the Inca roads to finish the job.
note: Documented.

claim: Spanish courts at first accepted khipus as evidence; keepers still read them.
note: True, including in colonial litigation.

claim: Church leaders ordered many cords burned (Third Council of Lima, 1583); fewer than 1,500 survive.
note: Around 900–1,000 known khipus in collections; estimates of ~1,000 or 'about a thousand'. 'Fewer than fifteen hundred' is true but inflated vs. common figure.
fix: 'Only about a thousand known khipus survive.'

claim: In 2014, UNESCO made Qhapaq Ñan a World Heritage Site across six countries.
note: Inscribed June 2014; Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru.

claim: Every June villagers near Cusco rebuild the grass bridge over the Apurímac.
note: Q'eswachaka, Canas province, renewal in early/mid June; it's a 3-day event. UNESCO intangible heritage (2013). It's near Cusco region (~100 km).
fix: 'in the Cusco region' ; say 'the last remaining Inca rope bridge'.

claim: On-screen: '240 KM A DAY' / '40,000 KM' captions.
note: Captions state estimates as fact; narration hedges.

claim: On-screen: 'CUSCO, PERU' image with 'red tile-free thatched roofs'; Inca capital.
note: Inca Cusco did have thatched roofs; description is confusingly worded ('tile-free'); avoid red tiles which are colonial.

claim: On-screen: 'CHILE, THE EDGE' and 'QUITO, ECUADOR' (map pins).
note: No numeric coordinates were shown; locations are correct. Maule is in central Chile.

claim: On-screen: '4,000 METERS' for the pass.
note: Matches narration (past four thousand meters).

claim: On-screen: '1532'.
note: Correct year for the Spanish arrival and Cajamarca.

claim: On-screen image: Inca runner with 'feathered headband' and Sapa Inca 'fine red tunic with fringed headband'.
note: Sapa Inca wore the red mascapaicha fringe; the runners' look is plausible but invented.
